Genome-wide analysis of the SWEET gene
family and its response to powdery mildew
and leaf spot infection in the common oat
(Avena sativa L.)
Yuanbo Pan<sup>1</sup>, Kuiju Niu<sup>1*</sup>, Peiqin Miao<sup>1</sup>, Guiqin Zhao<sup>1</sup>, Yuehua Zhang<sup>2</sup>, Zeliang Ju<sup>3</sup>, Jikuan Chai<sup>1</sup>, Juanjuan Yang<sup>1</sup>,
Xiaoning Cui<sup>1</sup> and Ran Zhang<sup>4</sup>
Abstract
The nutritional quality and yield of oats (Avena sativa) are often compromised by plant diseases such as red leaf,
powdery mildew, and leaf spot. Sugars Will Eventually be Exported Transporters (SWEETs) are newly identified
sugar transporters involved in regulating plant growth and stress responses. However, the roles of SWEET genes
in biotic stress responses remain uncharacterized in oats. In this study, 13 AsSWEET genes were identified across
nine chromosomes of the oat genome, all of which were predicted to contain seven transmembrane regions.
Phylogenetic analysis revealed four clades of AsSWEET proteins, with high homology to SWEET proteins in the
Poaceae family. Collinearity analysis demonstrated strong relationships between oat and Zea mays SWEETs. Using
subcellular localization prediction tools, AsSWEET proteins were predicted to localize to the plasma membrane.
Promoter analysis revealed cis-acting elements associated with light response, growth, and stress regulation.
Six AsSWEET proteins were predicted to interact in a network centered on AsSWEET1a and AsSWEET11. Gene
expression analysis of two oat varieties, ‘ForagePlus’ and ‘Molasses’, indicated significant expression diferences in
several AsSWEET genes following infection with powdery mildew or leaf spot, including AsSWEET1a, AsSWEET1b,
AsSWEET2b, AsSWEET3a, AsSWEET11, and AsSWEET16. These SWEET genes are potential candidates for disease
resistance in oats. This study provides a foundation for understanding the regulatory mechanisms of AsSWEET
genes, particularly in response to powdery mildew and leaf spot, and ofers insights for enhancing oat molecular
breeding.

Introduction
In plants, sugars serve as the primary sources of carbon
and energy [1]. Sugars are also known to be important
signaling molecules. In mesophyll cells of higher plants,
chloroplasts can fix carbon by converting carbon diox-
ide into organic carbon through photosynthesis [2–4].
However, sugars cannot be transported independently
through plant cell membrane systems, requiring the
assistance of appropriate sugar transporters [2]. Three
main types of sugar transport proteins have been iden-
tified: monosaccharide transporters (MSTs) [5], sucrose
transporters (SUTs) [6, 7], and Sugars Will Eventually be
Exported Transporters (SWEETs) [8]. In the past twenty
years, MSTs and SUTs have been widely studied in plants
[9]. The SWEET family genes play important roles in
transporting hexose and sucrose across cell membranes
[10], though their specific functions remain largely
unknown.
SWEETs are widely distributed in both eukaryotes
and prokaryotes. They are a type of sugar transport pro-
tein that does not depend on environmental pH values.
Eukaryotic SWEET proteins typically consist of seven
alpha-helical transmembrane domains (7-TMs), which
are folded into two 3-TM domains (conserved MtN3/
saliva domains) connected by one central TM [11].
SWEETs have been reported to be involved in regulat-
ing the response of plants to biotic stress. When plants
are invaded by bacterial or fungal pathogens, the patho-
gens obtain the necessary sugars from the plants, thereby
triggering the up-regulation of SWEET gene expression
[12, 13]. In the sweet potato, expression of IbSWEET10
was elevated after infection with Fusarium oxysporum
Schlecht. f. sp. Batatas; IbSWEET10 overexpression
resulted in resistance to this pathogen, and RNAi of
IbSWEET10 produced the opposite efect [14]. In Vitis
vinifera, VvSWEET4 has been found to interact with the
fungal pathogen Botrytis cinerea [15]. GhSWEET42 was
found to be up-regulated in Gossypium spp infected with
Verticillium dahlia [16]. Overexpression of GhSWEET42
resulted in increased susceptibility, whereas GhSWEET42
deficiency increased resistance. Similarly, in V. vinifera,
VvSWEET7 expression was induced by pathogens, con-
tributing to plant defense via removal of pathogen-syn-
thesized mannitol from the apoplast [17]. The roles of
endogenous sugars in mediating plant immune responses
and combating pathogen attacks are receiving increasing
attention, leading to the emergence of concepts such as
“sweet immunity” or “sugar enhanced defense” [18, 19].
Regulating these sugar levels will be significant for crop
improvement.
Oats (Avena sativa) are an important annual cereal and
feed crop in the Poaceae family [20]. Due to their strong
stress resistance, excellent quality, high yield, good palat-
ability, easy harvesting, and straightforward processing
and modulation, oats are a globally cultivated crop [21].
Oats are mainly produced in Russia, Canada, the United
States, Australia, Germany, Finland, China, and several
other nations in the northern hemisphere [22]. Global
population growth and the increasing demand for nutri-
tious and healthy foods have led to annual increases in
oat production [23]. With changes in climate and envi-
ronmental conditions, oat cultivation has been threat-
ened by diseases such as powdery mildew, red leaf
disease, smut, and leaf spot, which have inhibited the
quality and yield of oats in recent years [24, 25]. Cur-
rently, fungal plant diseases in oats are controlled using
methods such as field cultivation management, biological
control, chemical control, and the breeding of resistant
varieties [26]. However, cultivation management is time-
consuming and labor-intensive, and chemical control
can easily lead to environmental pollution [27]. Thus, the
identification and characterization of genes involved in
disease susceptibility and resistance are necessary to pro-
vide a basis for the genetic improvement of crops.
Thus far, numerous studies have shown that SWEET
sugar transporters are closely associated with biotic and
abiotic stress responses in plants [28–30], but few of
these studies have characterized the roles of oat SWEETs
in response to biotic stress. Therefore, this study aimed
to identify the oat SWEET family genes and system-
atically analyze the structural characteristics, conserved
protein motifs and structures, and the expression of
these SWEET genes in oat leaves under diferent disease
stresses. This study provides a theoretical basis for under-
standing the role of SWEET genes in regulating plant
disease resistance, thereby facilitating the exploration of
superior oat genetic resources and the development of
new cultivars.

structures

33.59%. β-turn structures were the smallest contributors
in all AsSWEET proteins. The proportions of extended
chains fluctuated, ranging from 13.74 to 25.30%. Predic-
tions of tertiary structures of AsSWEET proteins (Fig. 2)
indicated that the tertiary structures of AsSWEET1a and
AsSWEET1b were highly similar, as were the tertiary
structures of AsSWEET2a and AsSWEET2b. The pre-
dicted tertiary structures of the remaining proteins had
significant diferences, though α-helical structures were
the main structural component in all.

Identification of cis-acting elements in AsSWEETs
The cis-acting elements identified in the promoter
regions of the AsSWEETs were associated with light
response, growth and development, hormone response,
and abiotic stress response (Fig.  5C). All 13 AsSWEET
genes contained at least one and up to nine photores-
ponsive elements. Ten genes contained between one and
four auxin-responsive elements, and 12 genes contained
between one and four gibberellin-responsive elements.

Phylogenetic analysis indicated that the SWEET pro-

8) are mainly involved in transporting glucose, fructose,

olar membranes [40]. In this study, oat AsSWEETs were

Conclusion
In this study, a total of 13 SWEET sugar transporter
proteins were identified in the oat, distributed across
nine chromosomes in the oat genome. All AsSWEET
sugar transporters were predicted to be hydrophobic
proteins containing 7 TMHs. Both secondary and ter-
tiary structure predictions indicated α-helices as the
main structural components of the AsSWEET proteins.
Phylogenetic analysis indicated that AsSWEET proteins
clustered into four subfamilies, with high homology
to the SWEET protein families of multiple crops in the
Poaceae family. AsSWEET promoter regions contained
cis-acting elements related to light response, growth and
development, and stress response. SWEET genes from
oats and O. sativa were found to have strong collinear
relationships. Six AsSWEET proteins were predicted to
interact with each other in a network centered around
AsSWEET1a and AsSWEET11. The AsSWEETs actively
participated in the response to biological stress. Among
them, AsSWEET1a, 1b, 2b, 3a, 11, and 16 were diferen-
tially expressed after infection with either powdery mil-
dew or leaf spot, making them important candidate genes
for studying the oat response to biological stress.
